topic: reslating a roof in second hand slate: sizing courses, headlap on a slack pitch, nails and ridge bedding

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-6)
provenance.notes: pisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: katomierz spadku dachu odczytujacy stopnie

base: I am reslating the back of the house with second hand Welsh slate and sorting it into sizes.
The porch roof was slated by my father in the seventies and has never let in water.
A pitch gauge sits in my bag and reads the fall of every roof I look at.
The slates run from large ones at the eaves down to small ones near the ridge.
Do I really need to grade them that way, or would one size do throughout?
Grade them, because sizing the courses is what lets old slate cover a roof without waste.
The largest slates carry the most water at the eaves and want the greatest strength there.
Diminishing courses also lift the eye and make a plain roof look considerably better.
Sort the whole load into five or six sizes before you set a single batten.
I sorted the load into six sizes and holed the ones that had lost their holes.
The pitch gauge reads twenty six degrees, which is a good deal lower than I assumed.
Someone told me that the pitch decides the headlap, though I do not see quite why.
How much lap should I be giving at that fall, and does slate size change it?
Twenty six degrees is low for slate, so give a lap of at least four inches.
Water travels further up under the slate on a slack pitch than on a steep one.
Small slates near the ridge want the same lap, which is why the batten gauge tightens.
Work the gauge out for each size separately and mark the battens before you fix any.
I worked out a gauge for each of the six sizes and marked the battens accordingly.
The eaves course is doubled and the first three courses lie beautifully flat.
The porch roof has the same doubled eaves, which I had never once understood before.
I have been nailing with galvanised nails because they came with the batten order.
Will those last as long as the slate, or should I have bought copper instead?
Galvanised nails will not last as long as the slate, and that is the usual reason roofs fail.
The slate outlives the fixing, so the roof comes down while every slate is still sound.
Copper costs more at the start and is the cheaper of the two over a century.
Aluminium is a fair middle course and is rather easier to drive into hard batten.
Whatever you use, drive the nail so the head just touches and never pulls the slate.
I changed to copper nails for the rest of the roof and the driving is much easier.
Two slates cracked as I nailed them, both of them near the middle of a course.
The holes had been punched by hand and are perhaps a little close to the head.
Should I be reholing the old slates, or is a cracked one in ten simply expected?
Rehole them, since an old hole in the wrong place will crack far more than one in ten.
Punch from the back so the hole leaves a countersink on the face for the nail head.
Set the hole a third of the way down from the head, not right up at the top.
A nail too near the head levers the slate every time the wind lifts the tail.
Reholing from the back cured it and I have not cracked a slate since then.
The roof is up to the ridge and I am left with the ridge tiles to bed.
There is a good deal of talk about mortar bedding against the dry ridge systems.
On an old roof like this one, which of the two would you actually choose?
On a roof of this age I would bed in lime mortar rather than anything modern.
Cement bedding is hard, cracks away from the tile and takes the slate with it.
Lime moves with the timber and can be raked out and repointed in fifty years.
Bed the tiles on a full mortar bed with slate slips to keep the joints from sinking.
